newsitem.title: USA: USDA increases soy output but stocks remain tight.
newsitem.headline: USDA increases soy output but stocks remain tight.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Department increased its estimate for U.S. soybean production Tuesday, but supplies remain tight, analysts said.
"When you look at the world numbers on beans, they're really not all that negative," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities in Des Moines, Iowa. "We changed just mildly our ending stocks."
USDA raised its U.S. soybean production estimate by 57 million bushels to 2.403 billion bushels but ending stocks grew by only 15 million bushels to 210 million.

"The increases in corn and beans are a little bigger than anyone thought," said Mark Cermak, oilseeds trading specialist with O'Connor and Co. "You've got a 210 carryout and that's almost comfortable."
Soybean futures at Chicago Board of Trade opened sharply lower on Tuesday following USDA's increased U.S. production figures. But the market turned higher, due in part to strong USDA demand data.
USDA increased export usage to 870 million bushels from 850 million on last month's report. Soybean crushings were raised to 1.390 billion bushels from 1.375 billion last month.

"I thought the USDA was a little aggressive there," said Everen Securities analyst Joel Karlin, referring to the usage figures. "They bumped the Chinese expected imports up by a good bit and lowered the Argentine crop. That helped them pick up some demand."
USDA projected China would import one million tonnes of soybeans, against last month's estimate of 900,000 tonnes.
The report also suggested China would buy 1.6 million tonnes of soymeal, compared with last month's estimate of 1.4 million tonnes.
USDA said Argentina's soybean crop would total 13 million tonnes, against last month's projection of 13.5 million.
"People are impressed by the demand for soybeans," Karlin said. "I think both corn and beans have hit their lows."
